articles.title: What Is Coordination of Benefits? How Two Health Plans Actually Pay a Claim
articles.description: Coordination of benefits decides which health plan pays first when you have two. Learn the birthday rule, primary vs. secondary, and how claims split.
articles.author: Insurance Bhaiya Research Desk
keyTakeaways: Coordination of benefits (COB) is the set of rules health plans use to decide which plan pays first (primary) and which pays what's left (secondary) when someone is covered by more than one plan.
COB exists specifically to prevent double payment: combined payments from both plans generally can't exceed the actual cost of the care, keeping insurance aligned with the principle of indemnity.

For a dependent child covered by both parents' plans, the 'birthday rule' usually decides which parent's plan is primary: whichever parent's birthday falls earlier in the calendar year (month and day only, not year).

COBRA continuation coverage is secondary to an active employer-sponsored plan, and a non-health payer like auto accident insurance or workers' compensation is usually primary over health insurance for a related claim.

faqs.question: Does coordination of benefits apply to Medicare?
faqs.answer: Yes, in a modified form — Medicare has its own coordination rules, often called Medicare Secondary Payer rules, that determine when Medicare pays first versus when an employer plan or other coverage pays first.

faqs.question: What happens if I don't tell my insurer about my other health plan?
faqs.answer: Claims can be delayed or initially processed incorrectly, since the primary plan may not know to expect a secondary payer. Most plans ask about other coverage during enrollment or claims processing specifically to apply COB correctly.

content.text: If you're covered by two health insurance plans at once, something has to decide which one actually pays first and how much each one covers. That something is coordination of benefits (COB), and understanding it is the key to answering [can you have two health insurances](/qa/can-you-have-two-health-insurances/) without assuming it means double payment.
The Basic Mechanism: Primary Pays First, Secondary Fills the Gap

The primary plan processes your claim as though it were your only coverage. The secondary plan then evaluates what's left, covering some or all of the remaining eligible amount, provided it's also a covered expense under that plan's own terms. Combined, the two plans generally can't pay more than the actual bill — COB is what prevents overpayment, not what creates it.

rows: Provider bills the primary plan first
Primary plan pays its normal share, as if it were the only coverage
Remaining eligible balance is submitted to the secondary plan
Secondary plan covers some or all of the rest, up to its own limits and covered-expense rules
Combined payment from both plans generally can't exceed the actual cost of care

content.text: How Primary vs. Secondary Is Decided

items: **For you:** your own employer-sponsored plan is typically primary for you.
**For your spouse:** their own employer-sponsored plan is typically primary for them.
**For dependent children:** the birthday rule usually applies (see below).
**COBRA vs. active coverage:** if you have COBRA continuation coverage plus another active employer-sponsored plan, the active employer plan is primary and COBRA is secondary.
**No clear rule applies:** the plan that has covered you longer is typically treated as primary.
**Non-health payers:** for injuries covered by something like auto accident insurance or workers' compensation, that non-health payer is usually primary over your regular health plan.

content.text: The Birthday Rule, Explained

When a dependent child is covered under both parents' health plans, insurers need a consistent way to decide whose plan pays first. The birthday rule, developed by the National Association of Insurance Commissioners, resolves this by comparing birthdays: whichever parent's birthday (month and day only — the birth year doesn't matter) falls earlier in the calendar year has the primary plan for the child. If both parents share a birthday, the plan that has covered either parent longer is usually treated as primary. For divorced or separated parents, a custody order or court decree often overrides the birthday rule entirely, typically prioritizing the custodial parent's plan first.

content.title: Tell Both Insurers About Your Other Coverage
content.text: COB only works correctly if both plans know about each other. Disclose other coverage when you enroll and whenever it changes (marriage, divorce, a new job, a child aging off a plan), since undisclosed coverage is one of the most common reasons COB claims get delayed.
What Coordination of Benefits Is Not

COB is not a way to get paid twice, and it's not the same as [multiple life insurance policies](/qa/can-i-have-multiple-life-insurance-policies/) paying independently — life insurance has no coordination at all because a death benefit isn't reimbursement for a variable loss. COB is also different from [subrogation](/glossary/subrogation/), where an insurer recovers money from an at-fault third party after paying a claim; COB coordinates between your own plans, while subrogation involves someone else's liability.

This article is educational and is not insurance or legal advice. Exact coordination of benefits rules vary by state, plan type, and specific plan documents; confirm your own plans' COB provisions with each insurer or your benefits administrator.

articles.title: Can You Have Multiple Insurance Policies at Once? Health, Life, Auto, and Disability
articles.description: Yes, you can have multiple insurance policies, but the rules differ by type. See how health, life, auto, and disability coverage stack.
articles.author: Insurance Bhaiya Research Desk
tags: can you have two health insurances
can i have multiple life insurance policies
keyTakeaways: Yes, you can generally hold more than one insurance policy of almost any type, but what happens when you file a claim differs sharply by line of coverage.

Health insurance uses coordination of benefits (COB): both plans can pay, but combined payments can't exceed 100% of the actual bill, and a primary/secondary order (often the birthday rule for kids) decides who pays first.

Life insurance has no legal limit and no coordination at all — each policy pays its full death benefit independently — but insurers cap total coverage using income-based financial underwriting, commonly 20 to 30 times annual income depending on age.
Auto insurance is legal to double up on, but the indemnity principle means you can't collect twice for the same loss, and most insurers won't knowingly insure the same car twice.
Disability insurance can be stacked across carriers, but insurers coordinate so your combined monthly benefit typically can't exceed roughly 60-70% of your income, whether from one policy or several.

faqs.question: Is it illegal to have two insurance policies of the same type?
faqs.answer: No. Owning multiple policies of the same type is legal across health, life, auto, and disability insurance. What's restricted is collecting more than your actual loss on an indemnity-based policy, or misrepresenting your coverage to an insurer.

faqs.question: Does having multiple policies mean I get paid twice?
faqs.answer: Only for life insurance, where each policy pays its full death benefit independently. For health, auto, and disability insurance, coordination and indemnity rules generally cap your total payout at your actual loss or a set percentage of income, not a doubled amount.

content.text: "Can you have multiple insurance policies" doesn't have one answer, because the rules depend entirely on which type of insurance you mean. Health insurance coordinates so you don't collect twice. Life insurance stacks in full, with no coordination, subject only to an income-based ceiling. Auto and disability sit in between. This guide covers all four, plus the coordination of benefits mechanism that makes dual health coverage actually work.
Can You Have Two Health Insurances?

Yes. It's common for a working spouse to be covered by their own employer plan and their spouse's plan, or for a child to be listed on both parents' plans. When you have two health plans, coordination of benefits (COB) rules decide which plan pays first (primary) and which pays what's left (secondary), so the total paid never exceeds the actual bill. Full answer, including the birthday rule for kids: [can you have two health insurances](/qa/can-you-have-two-health-insurances/).
What Is Coordination of Benefits?

Coordination of benefits is the mechanism, not a form of double coverage — it exists specifically to prevent double-dipping. The primary plan pays as if it were your only coverage; the secondary plan then covers some or all of what's left, up to its own limits. See the full mechanics, including how [COBRA](/glossary/cobra-continuation-coverage/) and Medicare fit in, at [what is coordination of benefits](/learn/what-is-coordination-of-benefits/).
Can I Have Multiple Life Insurance Policies?

Yes, and there's no legal limit on how many you can own. Unlike health insurance, life insurance doesn't coordinate: if you have three valid, in-force policies when you die, all three pay their full death benefit. The real constraint is financial [underwriting](/learn/what-is-insurance-underwriting/) — insurers cap total coverage as a multiple of your income (roughly 20 to 30 times, depending on your age) and check the MIB database for your existing coverage when you apply for more. Full answer: [can i have multiple life insurance policies](/qa/can-i-have-multiple-life-insurance-policies/).
Can You Have Two Auto Insurance Policies?

It's legal, but it rarely makes sense on the same car. Auto insurance follows the [indemnity principle](/glossary/principle-of-indemnity/): you can be reimbursed for your actual loss, not paid twice for it, so you can't file the same claim with two insurers and collect from both. Most insurers also decline to knowingly insure a vehicle that's already covered elsewhere. Two policies on two different vehicles is normal and unrelated to this question. Full answer: [can you have two auto insurance policies](/qa/can-you-have-two-auto-insurance-policies/).
Can You Have Multiple Disability Insurance Policies?

Yes, and this one is common on purpose: it's called "stacking," often used by high earners whose group long-term disability plan caps out well below what they'd need to replace their income. But it isn't unlimited stacking — insurers coordinate so your combined monthly benefit across all policies typically can't exceed about 60-70% of your income. Full answer: [can you have multiple disability insurance policies](/qa/can-you-have-multiple-disability-insurance-policies/).

rows: Coordination of benefits — combined payout capped at 100% of the bill
Each policy pays its full death benefit independently, no coordination
Legal, but rarely useful on one car
Can't collect twice for the same loss (indemnity principle)
Combined monthly benefit typically capped around 60-70% of income

content.title: The Pattern Behind All Four
content.text: Health and disability insurance are indemnity-based (they replace an actual loss, so insurers coordinate to prevent overpayment). Life insurance is not indemnity-based (a death benefit is a fixed sum, not a reimbursement), which is exactly why it can stack in full with no coordination at all.

If you're weighing whether to add a second life policy instead of raising your current one, see [how much life insurance do I need](/qa/how-much-life-insurance-do-i-need/) and [is life insurance an asset](/qa/is-life-insurance-an-asset/) in our [Life Insurance Fundamentals guide](/learn/life-insurance-fundamentals-worth-it-payouts-ownership/). For the auto side, [is car insurance cheaper on older cars](/qa/is-car-insurance-cheaper-on-older-cars/) and our [Car Insurance Basics guide](/learn/car-insurance-basics-registration-cost-claims/) cover related ground, and [independent agency vs. direct insurer](/compare/agency-vs-direct-insurance/) is useful if you're shopping a second policy through a different channel.

articles.title: Workers' Compensation Insurance Exemptions: Who Doesn't Have to Carry It, and What That Means If You Get Hurt
articles.description: Which businesses and workers are exempt from mandatory workers' compensation coverage, why life insurance agents are a special case, and what actually protects your income if you're hurt on a job that has no workers' comp behind it.
articles.author: Insurance Bhaiya Research Desk
keyTakeaways: Workers' compensation is mandatory in every state except Texas once a business crosses a state-specific employee-count threshold, but a long list of exceptions - sole proprietors, many LLC members, electing corporate officers, and commission-only agents - fall outside that requirement even in states that otherwise mandate it.

Several states carve out licensed insurance agents, including life insurance agents, the same way they carve out real estate agents, when the agent is paid solely by commission under a written contract - but this is a state-by-state rule, not a federal one, and it is easy to get wrong.

Calling someone an independent contractor does not make them exempt. States apply a control test, and a worker treated like an employee in practice can be ruled one after an injury, regardless of what the contract says.

Texas is the only state where workers' compensation is genuinely optional for almost every private employer - opting out is called becoming a non-subscriber, and it trades statutory immunity from lawsuits for full exposure to negligence claims.

Exemption does not mean protection disappears - it means the protection has to come from somewhere else, which is exactly the gap that individual disability insurance and occupational accident insurance exist to fill.

faqs.question: If I'm exempt from workers' compensation, am I automatically uninsured if I get hurt at work?
faqs.answer: Not automatically, but you do lose the specific protection workers' comp provides - guaranteed medical coverage and partial wage replacement regardless of fault. Your own health insurance may cover the medical bills, though some plans exclude work-related injuries, and your income is only protected if you separately carry individual disability insurance or an occupational accident policy.

faqs.question: Can a business that is exempt from workers' compensation still buy it voluntarily?
faqs.answer: Yes. Many exempt owners buy a small voluntary policy anyway, sometimes called a ghost policy for a sole proprietor, either to protect themselves financially or because a general contractor or client requires proof of coverage before signing a contract.

faqs.question: Does an exemption from workers' compensation ever get challenged after an injury?
faqs.answer: Frequently. Misclassifying an employee as an independent contractor, or misunderstanding a corporate-officer election, are among the most common reasons an exemption is challenged and reversed after a claim is filed, sometimes with penalties on top of the unpaid premium.

content.text: Workers' compensation exists to answer one question fast: who pays if a worker is hurt on the job? For most employers the answer is a mandatory policy. But a meaningful list of workers and business owners fall outside that requirement entirely, and the reasons range from how a business is structured to how a specific worker is paid. This guide walks through who is commonly exempt, why [life insurance](/learn/what-is-life-insurance/) agents are a genuinely special case, and - because this sits in our disability-insurance category for a reason - what actually protects your income when workers' comp isn't there to catch you.
The General Rule, and the One State That Breaks It

Every state except Texas requires most employers to carry workers' compensation once they cross a state-specific employee threshold - commonly as low as one employee in New York, three in states like Georgia and Arkansas, or five in others. Coverage typically pays medical bills and a portion of lost wages for a work injury regardless of who was at fault, and in exchange the injured worker generally cannot sue the employer - the trade-off is often called the exclusive remedy. Texas is the outlier: private employers there can choose not to carry workers' comp at all, a choice covered in depth in [Marcus's Texas non-subscriber scenario](/scenarios/marcus-texas-non-subscriber-workers-comp/) below.
Who Is Commonly Exempt, Even in States That Require Coverage

Exemptions cluster around a few recurring categories. [Sole proprietors and business partners](/qa/are-sole-proprietors-required-to-have-workers-compensation-insurance/) are usually not required to cover themselves, only any employees they hire. Members of an LLC are frequently treated the same way as sole proprietors in single-member or small multi-member setups. Corporate officers can often elect out of coverage for themselves, typically limited to two to four officers who each hold a minimum ownership stake, with the exact number and percentage set by state law. Agricultural and seasonal farm labor is exempt in many states below a certain headcount, domestic workers in a private home are frequently exempt below an hours or wage threshold, and religious or certain nonprofit workers carry their own state-specific carve-outs.

rows: Must still cover any employees they hire
Rules tighten once employees are added
Usually capped at 2-4 officers with minimum ownership
Must pass the state's control test, not just a written label
Paid solely by commission, under a written contract

content.text: Are Life Insurance Agents Exempt From Workers' Compensation?

This is a narrower and more specific question than it first appears, and the full answer lives in [our dedicated Q&A](/qa/are-life-insurance-agents-exempt-from-workers-compensation/). The short version: the IRS's federal statutory nonemployee category covers direct sellers, licensed real estate agents and certain companion sitters - insurance agents are not on that federal list. But several states write their own, separate workers' compensation exemption for insurance agents (life, property and casualty alike) paid solely by commission under a written contract, using language that closely mirrors how they treat real estate agents. That means a life insurance agent's exemption status genuinely depends on the state they work in and the structure of their contract with the agency or carrier, not on a single nationwide rule - which matters both for someone [starting and running an insurance agency](/learn/starting-and-running-an-insurance-agency/) and for the agents that agency contracts with.
Independent Contractors: Exempt on Paper, Not Always in Practice

A written independent contractor agreement is a starting point, not the final word. States apply a control test - how much say the business has over hours, methods, tools and supervision - and a worker who looks like an employee in practice can be reclassified as one after an injury, even if both sides signed a contract calling them a contractor. This is one of the most common and expensive ways an exemption gets challenged, sometimes years after the fact and with back [premiums](/glossary/premium/) and penalties attached. Anyone relying on contractor status as a workers' comp exemption should read [the full independent contractor breakdown](/qa/are-independent-contractors-exempt-from-workers-compensation/) before assuming the label alone settles the question.

content.title: How many employees actually triggers the requirement?
content.text: The threshold is set state by state and is one of the most-asked follow-up questions once someone learns exemptions exist. [This breakdown by employee count](/qa/how-many-employees-before-you-need-workers-compensation-insurance/) covers the common ranges and why the number alone doesn't tell the whole story.
The Gap Exemption Creates - and What Actually Fills It

Being exempt from workers' compensation does not make a workplace injury disappear, it just removes the specific safety net workers' comp provides. [What actually happens if you're hurt at work with no workers' comp behind you](/qa/hurt-at-work-employer-exempt-from-workers-compensation/) depends on your own health insurance, whether it excludes work-related injuries, and whether you carry individual [disability insurance](/insurance/disability-insurance/) or an occupational accident policy to replace lost income. This is the real reason this topic sits in our disability-insurance category rather than purely under commercial or liability insurance: workers' comp and individual disability insurance are solving the same underlying problem - lost income after an injury - through two very different mechanisms, which [our side-by-side comparison](/compare/workers-compensation-vs-individual-disability-insurance/) lays out directly. Use the [Disability Insurance Needs Calculator](/disability-insurance-calculator/) to see what monthly benefit would actually replace your income if that gap ever became real.
Buying Workers' Comp Anyway: Voluntary Coverage and Ghost Policies

Exemption is a choice for many owners, not an obligation to go without coverage. A sole proprietor or exempt corporate officer can often buy a small voluntary policy, sometimes nicknamed a ghost policy, purely to protect their own finances after an injury. It's also common practice for a reason that has nothing to do with personal risk tolerance: many general contractors and larger clients will not sign a contract with a subcontractor or vendor who cannot produce a certificate of workers' comp coverage, exempt or not, because the client wants to avoid being treated as a statutory employer if something goes wrong - a concern covered from the client's own liability side in [quotes for commercial insurance](/learn/quotes-for-commercial-insurance/).
Which of These Questions Are Covered in Depth Elsewhere?

articles.title: Renters Insurance: What's Covered & What's Not
articles.description: A plain-language, question-by-question guide to what a standard renters insurance policy actually pays for — and the specific situations, like mold, floods, and roommates' belongings, where it doesn't.
articles.author: Insurance Bhaiya Home Insurance Group
keyTakeaways: A standard renters insurance policy bundles three core protections: personal property coverage (your belongings), personal liability coverage (injuries or damage you or your pet cause to others), and additional living expenses (a hotel bill if your unit becomes unlivable).

Personal property coverage generally follows your belongings wherever they go, including a bike stolen off a public rack or a laptop stolen from a coffee shop, subject to your policy's off-premises limit — commonly around 10% of your total personal property coverage.

The most common and most expensive gaps aren't obscure edge cases: flood and earthquake damage are excluded from nearly every standard policy, and gradual issues like mold from long-term neglect are treated very differently from mold caused by a sudden, covered leak.

Renters insurance and a landlord's own insurance cover two completely different things — the landlord's policy protects the building structure, not your belongings or your personal liability, which is exactly why renters insurance exists as a separate, necessary product.

Almost every specific 'does renters insurance cover X?' question in this space traces back to one of a small number of underlying rules: what counts as a named peril, what's excluded outright, what has a sub-limit, and who is actually named on the policy.

faqs.question: Is renters insurance legally required?
faqs.answer: Not by state law in most places, but many landlords and leases require it as a condition of renting, which functions as a practical requirement for a large share of tenants even where it isn't a legal mandate.

faqs.question: How much does renters insurance typically cost?
faqs.answer: Renters insurance is generally inexpensive relative to other insurance types, often costing a modest amount per month for a standard policy, though the exact cost depends on your coverage amount, location, and deductible.

faqs.question: Does renters insurance cover my belongings if my roommate causes the damage?
faqs.answer: This depends on the specific circumstances and your policy — damage caused by a roommate who isn't named on your policy can create coverage complications, which is covered in more detail in [Does Renters Insurance Cover Roommates' Belongings?](/qa/does-renters-insurance-cover-roommates-belongings/)

content.text: Renters insurance is inexpensive, widely underused, and surprisingly misunderstood — most people either assume it covers almost nothing beyond a break-in, or assume it covers almost everything the way [homeowners insurance](/learn/home-insurance-fundamentals/) does. Neither is quite right. This guide walks through exactly what a standard policy includes, using the same question-and-answer format as each linked page, so you can find your specific situation quickly.
What Does a Standard Renters Insurance Policy Actually Include?

Nearly every renters policy bundles three distinct coverages: personal property coverage, which pays to repair or replace your belongings after a covered loss like fire, theft, or [vandalism](/qa/does-car-insurance-cover-vandalism/); personal liability coverage, which pays if you, a family member, or a pet injures someone or damages their property, plus your legal defense costs if you're sued; and additional living expenses (ALE) coverage, which pays for a hotel and related costs if a covered loss makes your rental temporarily unlivable. Understanding which of these three buckets a specific claim falls into is the fastest way to predict whether it's covered.
Does Coverage Follow Your Belongings Outside the Apartment?

Yes, generally — personal property coverage isn't limited to things inside your unit. A bike [stolen from a public rack](/qa/does-renters-insurance-cover-bike-theft/), a laptop stolen from a coffee shop, or luggage stolen while traveling are all typically covered the same way as something stolen from inside your home, just subject to an off-premises [sub-limit](/glossary/sub-limit/), commonly around 10% of your total personal property coverage. This surprises a lot of renters who assume coverage stops at their front door.
What Are the Gaps That Actually Catch People Off Guard?

The most expensive surprises in [renters insurance](/qa/does-renters-insurance-cover-theft-outside-home/) aren't obscure — they're a small number of well-known, consistently excluded categories. [Flood and earthquake damage](/qa/does-renters-insurance-cover-flood-or-earthquake-damage/) are excluded from nearly every standard policy and require separate coverage. [Mold](/qa/does-renters-insurance-cover-mold/) is covered only when it results directly from a sudden, covered peril — not from long-term humidity or neglected maintenance. And [water damage from a leak](/qa/does-renters-insurance-cover-water-damage-from-a-leak/) depends heavily on whether the leak was sudden and accidental or a slow, known problem.

content.text: How Is This Different From What My Landlord's Insurance Covers?

A landlord's own property insurance protects the building itself — the structure, fixtures, and the landlord's own financial interest — and generally does nothing for your personal belongings or your personal liability as a tenant. This is one of the most common and costly misunderstandings among renters, and it's covered directly in [Renters Insurance vs. Landlord Insurance: Who Covers What?](/compare/renters-insurance-vs-landlord-insurance/)
How Much Coverage Do You Actually Need?

Rather than guessing, the right amount of personal property coverage is whatever it would actually cost to replace everything you own, which is usually higher than people initially estimate once clothing, furniture, and electronics are added up. See [How Much Renters Insurance Coverage Do You Actually Need?](/qa/how-much-renters-insurance-coverage-do-you-need/) for a practical way to estimate this rather than picking a number arbitrarily.

This article is educational and general in nature. Renters insurance coverage, exclusions, sub-limits, and state-specific rules vary significantly by insurer and policy. Always review your specific policy documents and consult a licensed insurance agent for guidance on your own coverage.

articles.title: New York State No-Fault Insurance Explained: $50,000 PIP, Deadlines & When You Can Sue
articles.description: New York no-fault insurance explained: what the $50,000 PIP covers, the 30-day deadline, the serious injury threshold, who's excluded and when you can sue.
articles.author: Insurance Bhaiya Research Desk
keyTakeaways: New York is a no-fault state. Your own policy's personal injury protection pays up to $50,000 per person in 'basic economic loss' after a crash, whoever caused it ([NY Insurance Law §5102](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/ISC/5102)).
That $50,000 covers medical bills, lost earnings up to $2,000 a month for up to three years, and up to $25 a day in other reasonable expenses for one year.

You must file your no-fault application within 30 days of the crash, submit medical bills within 45 days, and submit lost-wage claims within 90 days (per [NY DFS Regulation 68](https://www.dfs.ny.gov/apps_and_licensing/property_insurers/nofault_faqs_reg68)).

You can sue the at-fault driver for pain and suffering only if you meet New York's 'serious injury' [tort threshold](/glossary/tort-threshold/), such as a fracture, significant disfigurement or permanent limitation.
Car damage is still fault-based in New York. No-fault only covers injuries.

faqs.question: How does New York State no-fault insurance work?
faqs.answer: After a crash, your own insurer pays your medical bills, lost wages (up to $2,000 a month) and other expenses up to $50,000, whoever caused the crash. In exchange, you can only sue the at-fault driver for pain and suffering if you meet the serious injury threshold.

faqs.question: How long do I have to file a no-fault claim in New York?
faqs.answer: Thirty days from the crash to submit your no-fault application, 45 days for medical bills and 90 days for lost wages. Details are in [how to file a no-fault insurance claim in New York](/qa/how-to-file-a-no-fault-insurance-claim-in-new-york/).

faqs.question: Does New York no-fault cover car damage?
faqs.answer: No. Vehicle damage is handled by fault: the at-fault driver's property damage liability or your own collision coverage.

faqs.question: Does New York no-fault cover motorcycle accidents?
faqs.answer: Not for the motorcycle rider or passenger. Riders rely on MedPay, health insurance and the at-fault driver's liability. A pedestrian hit by a motorcycle, however, can generally claim no-fault benefits.

faqs.question: Can I sue after a no-fault accident in New York?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your injury is a 'serious injury' under Insurance Law §5102(d), such as a fracture, significant disfigurement or permanent limitation, or for economic losses above your no-fault benefits. See [tort threshold](/glossary/tort-threshold/).

content.text: If you drive in New York, **no-fault insurance** is the first thing that kicks in after a crash. It's also the part of the system people misunderstand most. It doesn't mean nobody is blamed, and it doesn't pay to fix your car. What it does is make your own insurer pay your medical bills and lost wages quickly, up to $50,000, without waiting to sort out who caused the crash. In return, New York limits when you can sue for pain and suffering. This guide walks you through exactly what New York State no-fault covers, who it leaves out, and the deadlines that can cost you your benefits. It's part of our [no-fault vs at-fault car insurance states hub](/learn/no-fault-vs-at-fault-car-insurance-states/).
What New York No-Fault Insurance Covers

rows: Hospital, doctor, surgery, therapy, prescriptions, ambulance, X-rays, prosthetics
Part of the $50,000 total, paid under New York's fee schedule
Wages you lose because of the injury (generally 80% of earnings)
Up to $2,000 a month, for up to 3 years
Household help, transport to medical appointments and similar costs
Up to $25 a day, for up to 1 year
Paid to the estate if the injured person dies
Extra coverage for lost earnings or therapy

content.text: Source: [New York Insurance Law §5102](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/ISC/5102). Everything is subject to the overall $50,000 per-person limit (plus any optional coverage you buy). For how PIP works in general, see [personal injury protection (PIP)](/glossary/personal-injury-protection/).

content.title: $50,000 Goes Faster Than You Think
content.text: A trauma admission, surgery and three months of physical therapy can use up most of $50,000, and lost wages come out of the same pot. If you earn a good income or have a physically demanding job, ask about the optional extra $25,000 (OBEL). Check your overall exposure with [how to know if you are underinsured](/learn/how-to-know-if-you-are-underinsured/).
Who Is Covered, and Who Isn't

items: **Covered:** you and relatives living in your household (even as passengers in other cars, in most cases), passengers in your car, and pedestrians your car hits.

**Not covered by NY no-fault:** motorcycle riders and their passengers, who rely on MedPay, health insurance and the at-fault driver's liability instead. See [motorcycle insurance vs car insurance](/compare/motorcycle-insurance-vs-car-insurance/).
**Commonly excluded:** people injured while driving intoxicated, while committing a felony, while racing, or while knowingly riding in a stolen car.
**No-fault doesn't cover** vehicle damage. That's handled by fault, through the other driver's property damage liability or your own [collision coverage](/compare/comprehensive-vs-collision/).

content.text: New York's Minimum Car Insurance Requirements

items: **Bodily injury liability:** $25,000 per person and $50,000 per accident ($50,000/$100,000 for death)
**Property damage liability:** $10,000
**Personal injury protection (no-fault):** $50,000
**Uninsured motorist:** $25,000/$50,000

content.text: You can't register a car in New York without this coverage. See [do you need insurance to register a car in NY](/qa/do-you-need-insurance-to-register-a-car-in-ny/) and [can you drive without insurance in NY](/qa/can-you-drive-without-insurance-in-ny/). A $10,000 property damage limit is very low for New York City traffic, so most drivers should raise it.
The Deadlines That Can Cost You Everything
New York no-fault is generous, but it's strict about timing. Under [DFS Regulation 68](https://www.dfs.ny.gov/apps_and_licensing/property_insurers/nofault_faqs_reg68):

items: **30 days:** submit written notice of claim (the no-fault application, form NF-2) to the insurer.
**45 days:** your medical providers must submit bills for treatment.
**90 days:** submit proof of lost earnings and other expenses.
**10 days:** file a DMV accident report (MV-104) if anyone was injured or property damage exceeds $1,000.

content.text: Insurers can deny late claims, although a reasonable justification for delay can sometimes rescue one. The full step-by-step process is in [how to file a no-fault insurance claim in New York](/qa/how-to-file-a-no-fault-insurance-claim-in-new-york/).
When Can You Sue in New York? The Serious Injury Threshold

No-fault replaces most small injury lawsuits. You can step outside it and sue the at-fault driver for pain and suffering, and for economic losses above $50,000, only if you have a **'serious injury'** under [Insurance Law §5102(d)](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/ISC/5102). That means death, dismemberment, significant disfigurement, a fracture, loss of a fetus, permanent loss of use of a body organ, member, function or system, permanent consequential limitation of use of a body organ or member, significant limitation of use of a body function or system, or an injury that prevents you from performing substantially all your usual daily activities for at least 90 of the 180 days after the crash. This kind of rule is called a verbal [tort threshold](/glossary/tort-threshold/).

Once you clear it, New York uses **pure comparative negligence**. You can recover even if you were partly at fault, reduced by your share ([Bloomberg Law chart](https://pro.bloomberglaw.com/insights/litigation/contributory-and-comparative-negligence-by-state/)). That's more forgiving than the 50% and 51% bars in at-fault states like [Georgia](/qa/is-georgia-a-no-fault-state/) and [Texas](/qa/is-texas-a-no-fault-state/).

content.title: Denied or Underpaid? You Have Options
content.text: If your no-fault insurer denies treatment or cuts off benefits (often after an independent medical exam), you can challenge it through no-fault arbitration or in court. See [what to do when an insurer denies or delays](/qa/can-i-sue-my-insurance-company-for-taking-too-long/), and consider [when to hire an insurance lawyer](/learn/when-to-hire-an-insurance-lawyer/).
New York No-Fault vs At-Fault States

Right to sue for pain and suffering
Optional PIP (TX) or MedPay (CO default $5,000). See [PIP vs MedPay](/compare/pip-vs-medpay/)

articles.title: No-Fault vs At-Fault Car Insurance States: Which One Is Yours and Who Pays After a Crash?
articles.description: No-fault vs at-fault car insurance states explained: the full list of no-fault states, how PIP and tort thresholds work, and who pays your bills after a crash.
articles.author: Insurance Bhaiya Research Desk
keyTakeaways: Twelve states use no-fault car insurance: Florida, Hawaii, Kansas, Kentucky, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, New York, North Dakota, Pennsylvania and Utah. The rest, including [Texas](/qa/is-texas-a-no-fault-state/), [Georgia](/qa/is-georgia-a-no-fault-state/) and [Colorado](/qa/is-colorado-a-no-fault-state/), are at-fault (tort) states.

In a no-fault state, your own [personal injury protection](/glossary/personal-injury-protection/) pays your medical bills first, whoever caused the crash. In an at-fault state, the driver who caused it (through their liability insurance) pays.
No-fault only covers injuries. Car damage is still decided by fault in every state.

You can step outside no-fault and sue only when your injuries pass a [tort threshold](/glossary/tort-threshold/). In New York that means a 'serious injury' as defined in law. See [New York no-fault insurance](/learn/new-york-no-fault-insurance/).

About 1 in 3 US drivers were uninsured or underinsured in 2023 ([IRC](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20250220231032/en/One-in-Three-US-Drivers-Are-Either-Uninsured-or-Underinsured-Exposing-Themselves-and-Other-Drivers-to-Significant-Financial-Risk-New-IRC-Study-Shows)). In an at-fault state, that makes your own uninsured motorist coverage your safety net. See [is uninsured motorist coverage required in Georgia](/qa/is-uninsured-motorist-coverage-required-in-georgia/).

faqs.question: Which states are no-fault states?
faqs.answer: Florida, Hawaii, Kansas, Kentucky, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, New York, North Dakota, Pennsylvania and Utah. Kentucky, New Jersey and Pennsylvania are 'choice' no-fault states, where you can pay more to keep full rights to sue.

faqs.question: Is no-fault insurance better than at-fault?
faqs.answer: Neither is simply better. No-fault pays injury bills faster and reduces small lawsuits, but limits your right to sue and tends to cost more. At-fault systems keep full lawsuit rights but can leave you waiting, or unpaid, if the other driver is uninsured or blame is disputed.

faqs.question: Does no-fault insurance cover car damage?
faqs.answer: No. No-fault (PIP) covers injuries. Vehicle damage is paid by the at-fault driver's property damage liability or your own collision coverage, in every state.

faqs.question: Can I sue in a no-fault state?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your injury meets the state's tort threshold (for example, New York's 'serious injury' categories), or for vehicle damage. See [tort threshold](/glossary/tort-threshold/).

faqs.question: If I'm in a crash in another state, whose rules apply?
faqs.answer: Generally the law of the state where the crash happened decides fault and lawsuit rights, while your own policy's coverages, such as PIP, follow you. Most policies automatically adjust to meet another state's minimums while you drive there.

content.text: Picture two crashes that are exactly alike. A driver runs a red light and T-bones you, and you walk away with a broken wrist and $9,000 in medical bills. In Houston you'd claim against the other driver's insurance and wait while fault gets sorted out. In Brooklyn you'd file with your own insurer within 30 days, and it would start paying your bills whoever was to blame. Same crash, very different process. That's the difference between **at-fault and no-fault car insurance states**, and it shapes what coverage you should buy, how fast you get paid and whether you can sue.

This hub explains both systems in plain English, lists every no-fault state, and links to state-by-state answers. If you're new to car insurance, start with our [car insurance guide](/learn/car-insurance-guide/) and [car insurance basics](/learn/car-insurance-basics-registration-cost-claims/), then come back here.
What Is a No-Fault State?

In a **no-fault state**, every driver must carry [personal injury protection (PIP)](/glossary/personal-injury-protection/). After a crash, your own PIP pays your medical bills, and usually some lost wages, no matter who caused it. Your passengers generally claim on your PIP too, and pedestrians you hit may be covered under it. The trade-off is that your right to sue the other driver for pain and suffering is limited. You can only sue when your injuries pass the state's [tort threshold](/glossary/tort-threshold/). The idea is faster payment for everyday injuries and fewer lawsuits over minor ones.
What Is an At-Fault (Tort) State?

In an **at-fault state**, the person who caused the crash is financially responsible, and so is their bodily injury liability insurance. You claim against the at-fault driver's insurer, or sue them, for medical bills, lost wages, pain and suffering and car damage. There's no threshold, so you can sue for any injury. The catch is that payment waits until fault is established, and if you were partly to blame, your payout may be cut or wiped out under your state's comparative negligence rule. That's why at-fault states lean on optional coverages such as [MedPay and PIP](/compare/pip-vs-medpay/) and uninsured motorist coverage to fill the gap.
The 12 No-Fault States (and Their PIP Minimums)

rows: PIP generally pays 80% of medical bills. Motorcycles aren't included. See [Florida motorcycle insurance](/qa/do-you-need-insurance-on-a-motorcycle-in-florida/)
Choice no-fault: you can reject tort limits
Tiered choice (opt-out possible with qualifying health cover)

content.text: Figures are based on [ValuePenguin's state-by-state no-fault summary](https://www.valuepenguin.com/no-fault-auto-insurance) and each state's insurance code. Thresholds and PIP options change, so confirm the current rules with your state insurance department. **Choice no-fault** states (Kentucky, New Jersey and Pennsylvania) let you keep full rights to sue in exchange for a higher [premium](/glossary/premium/).

content.title: No-Fault Doesn't Mean No Blame
content.text: This is the most common misunderstanding. No-fault only changes who pays for **injuries** first. Car damage is still decided by fault in every state: the at-fault driver's property damage liability pays for your car, or your own [collision coverage](/compare/comprehensive-vs-collision/) does. Fault also still goes on the at-fault driver's record and can raise their premium. See [how long an accident stays on your insurance](/qa/how-long-does-an-accident-stay-on-your-insurance/).
No-Fault vs At-Fault: Side-by-Side

rows: Who pays your injury bills first?
Your own PIP, regardless of fault
The at-fault driver's liability insurer, once fault is set (or your own MedPay, PIP or health insurance in the meantime)
Can you sue for pain and suffering?
Only if you pass the tort threshold
The at-fault driver (property damage liability) or your collision coverage
Bodily injury liability. PIP or MedPay optional or must be offered in some states
Can take months if fault is disputed
Often higher on average (PIP plus fraud costs)
Varies. Uninsured drivers push costs up

content.text: Comparative Fault: How Blame Gets Split in At-Fault States

Most crashes aren't 100/0. States split blame in one of three ways, and it decides whether you get paid at all. According to [Bloomberg Law's state-by-state negligence chart](https://pro.bloomberglaw.com/insights/litigation/contributory-and-comparative-negligence-by-state/):

items: **Modified comparative, 51% bar.** You recover damages reduced by your share of fault, but nothing if you're 51% or more to blame. Texas uses this rule. See [is Texas an at-fault state](/qa/is-texas-a-no-fault-state/).

**Modified comparative, 50% bar.** You recover nothing at 50% or more. Georgia and Colorado use versions of this rule. See [is Georgia a no-fault state](/qa/is-georgia-a-no-fault-state/) and [is Colorado a no-fault state](/qa/is-colorado-a-no-fault-state/).
**Pure comparative.** You recover something even if you're mostly at fault, reduced by your share. New York uses this rule for lawsuits that clear its no-fault threshold.
**Contributory negligence.** A handful of places bar recovery if you're even 1% at fault.

content.title: Be Careful What You Say to the Other Driver's Insurer
content.text: In at-fault states, adjusters use recorded statements to assign percentages of blame. A casual 'I didn't see him' can cost you 20% of your claim. Read [can I refuse a recorded statement to an insurance company](/qa/can-i-refuse-a-recorded-statement-to-insurance-company/) before you call them back.
The Uninsured Driver Problem (Both Systems)

The [Insurance Research Council](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20250220231032/en/One-in-Three-US-Drivers-Are-Either-Uninsured-or-Underinsured-Exposing-Themselves-and-Other-Drivers-to-Significant-Financial-Risk-New-IRC-Study-Shows) estimates that 15.4% of US drivers were uninsured in 2023 and 33.4% were either uninsured or underinsured. In an at-fault state, if the driver who hit you has no insurance, there's no liability policy to claim against. Your own **uninsured/underinsured motorist (UM/UIM)** coverage steps in. Some states require it, and others require insurers to include it unless you reject it in writing. Georgia is a good example, covered in [is uninsured motorist coverage required in Georgia](/qa/is-uninsured-motorist-coverage-required-in-georgia/) and in our real-life [Atlanta uninsured driver scenario](/scenarios/uninsured-driver-crash-georgia-um-claim/). For the legal side, see [can an insurance company sue an uninsured driver](/qa/can-an-insurance-company-sue-an-uninsured-driver/).
What Coverage Should You Buy in Each System?

items: **In a no-fault state:** Buy more than the minimum PIP if you can. New York's $50,000 goes fast after surgery. Carry solid bodily injury limits anyway, because serious crashes still end up in court. Learn the claim steps in [how to file a no-fault insurance claim in New York](/qa/how-to-file-a-no-fault-insurance-claim-in-new-york/).

**In an at-fault state:** Don't decline MedPay or PIP when your insurer offers it. It pays while fault is argued over. Compare the two in [PIP vs MedPay](/compare/pip-vs-medpay/). Colorado insurers must include $5,000 of MedPay unless you reject it in writing.

**Everywhere:** Carry UM/UIM matching your liability limits, liability of at least 100/300/100 if you have assets to protect, and an [umbrella policy](/learn/umbrella-insurance-guide/) once your net worth exceeds those limits. Check yourself with [how to know if you are underinsured](/learn/how-to-know-if-you-are-underinsured/).

California high fire risk home insurance
keyTakeaways: Home insurance is really a stack of layers - the building, the fixtures inside it, your belongings, and your liability - and the most expensive mistakes happen when you assume someone else's policy covers a layer that is actually yours.

If you own a leasehold flat in England or Wales, the freeholder almost always arranges the block buildings policy and you pay through your service charge, but you still need your own contents cover for everything inside the flat.

Body corporate (strata) insurance in Australia covers the building and common property, not your belongings or your liability inside your lot, so most owner-occupiers still need a contents policy and landlords need landlord cover.

A standard house policy pays for a boiler damaged by an insured event like fire or a storm, but not for a boiler that simply wears out - breakdown protection is a separate add-on, warranty or service plan.

In high-risk markets like Florida and California, roof age, wind or wildfire mitigation, and whether you are stuck in the state insurer of last resort (Citizens or the FAIR Plan) matter more to your premium than almost anything else on the application.

faqs.question: Does bundling home and auto insurance always save money?
faqs.answer: Usually, but not always. Multi-policy discounts commonly land somewhere between 5% and 25% depending on the insurer and state, yet the cheapest home policy and the cheapest auto policy sometimes come from two different companies. Price the bundle and the two separate policies side by side before assuming the bundle wins, and use the [Home Insurance Coverage Calculator](/home-insurance-calculator/) to make sure the home half is sized correctly first.

faqs.question: Is buildings insurance a legal requirement for a leasehold flat?
faqs.answer: Not by law in England and Wales, but it is almost always a condition of your lease and your mortgage. In practice the freeholder or managing agent arranges it for the whole block and the cost is recharged through your service charge, so check your lease to confirm who is responsible.

faqs.question: Can a standard home policy replace flood or earthquake cover?
faqs.answer: No. In the US, flood and earthquake damage are excluded from standard homeowners policies and need separate policies or endorsements, which is why the [replacement cost estimator](/home-replacement-cost-estimator/) and a written exclusions review belong in every renewal.

content.text: Searches about home insurance look scattered - someone in Florida wants quotes, someone in a London flat wonders whether they need their own buildings policy, someone in Brisbane asks whether the body corporate has them covered, and someone in California is trying to keep any coverage at all. Underneath, they are all asking the same question: which layer of this property is insured by whom, and what falls through the gap? This guide walks through seven of the most common versions of that question, with the mechanics that explain each answer. For the basic building blocks, the [Home Insurance Coverage Calculator](/home-insurance-calculator/) shows how a standard policy splits across dwelling, other structures, belongings, loss of use and liability.
Home and Auto Insurance Near Me: Is Bundling Worth It?

People who search for [home and auto insurance near me](/qa/home-and-auto-insurance-near-me/) are usually deciding between three routes: a captive agent who sells one company's products, an independent agent or broker who can quote several, or a direct online quote. Bundling a home and auto policy with the same insurer typically earns a multi-policy discount, commonly somewhere in the 5% to 25% range depending on the carrier and state, and it also means one claims relationship, one renewal date and one bill. The trade-off is that a bundle is only a bargain if the underlying rates are competitive, so always price the bundle against two separate policies. Sizing matters as much as price: a cheap bundle built on a dwelling limit that is too low is the costliest kind of savings, so run your numbers through the [Home Replacement-Cost Estimator](/home-replacement-cost-estimator/) first and read [agent vs broker vs insurer](/learn/agent-vs-broker-vs-insurer/) to understand who you are actually buying from. Some regional insurers, including several Farm Bureau companies, add an account discount when home and auto sit under the same membership - more on that [below](/qa/what-does-farm-bureau-homeowners-insurance-cover/).
Do I Need Building Insurance for a Leasehold Flat?

In England and Wales, a leasehold flat owner usually does not arrange [buildings insurance](/scenarios/alex-first-mortgage-london/) personally. The freeholder, a residents' management company or the managing agent buys one block policy covering the structure and common parts, and each leaseholder pays a share through the service charge. Buildings insurance is not required by statute, but it is normally required by the lease and by your mortgage lender, so the practical answer to [do I need building insurance for a leasehold flat](/qa/do-i-need-building-insurance-for-a-leasehold-flat/) is: you need it to exist, but you rarely need to buy it. What you do need is your own contents insurance, and ideally a policy that adds accidental damage to internal fixtures and trace-and-access cover for finding leaks. There is one important exception - if you share the freehold, the leaseholders arrange the block policy themselves, so read the insurance clause in your lease.
Do I Need Home Insurance If I Have Body Corporate?

The Australian version of the same question - [do I need home insurance if I have body corporate](/qa/do-i-need-home-insurance-if-i-have-body-corporate/) - has a similar answer. Body corporate (also called strata or owners corporation) insurance is compulsory for the scheme and covers the building, common property and the scheme's [public liability](/qa/contract-works-insurance-vs-public-liability-insurance/). It generally does not cover your furniture and belongings, certain internal items such as carpets, curtains and some fixtures depending on the state, or your personal liability inside your lot. Owner-occupiers therefore typically need a contents policy, and investors need landlord insurance. Excess rules also catch people out: when damage affects only one lot, the lot owner may be asked to pay the excess, and a leak that originates in your unit can leave you responsible for the neighbour's claim.

rows: Everything: dwelling, belongings, liability, plus separate flood or earthquake cover if exposed
Freeholder or management company (block policy, paid via service charge)
Contents cover, ideally with accidental damage and trace-and-access
Contents cover (owners) or landlord insurance (investors), plus personal liability
Association master policy covers the building, per the bylaws
An HO-6 policy for interiors, belongings, liability and loss assessment

content.title: Read the insurance clause before you buy anything
content.text: In every one of these structures the answer to 'who insures the building?' is written in a document - your lease, your scheme's by-laws, your condo declaration or your mortgage terms. Five minutes with that clause settles the question better than any general guide, including this one. See the [Policy Review Checklist](/policy-review-checklist/) for a structured way to audit what you find.
Home Insurance Quotes in Hialeah: Why Two Neighbours Get Very Different Numbers

Anyone comparing [home insurance quotes in Hialeah](/scenarios/yesenia-hialeah-home-insurance-quotes/) is shopping in one of the most expensive property insurance markets in the country. Miami-Dade quotes are driven less by square footage than by roof age and material, the year the home was built, and how well it resists wind. Two inspections do most of the work: a 4-point inspection (roof, electrical, plumbing, HVAC), typically required for older homes, and a wind mitigation inspection, which commonly costs roughly $75 to $150 and can unlock meaningful credits on the wind portion of the premium. Many private carriers hesitate on shingle roofs beyond roughly 15 years, and the state insurer of last resort, [Citizens Property Insurance](/compare/florida-homeowners-insurance/), has been cutting rates in 2026 and depopulating back to private carriers - so compare private quotes against Citizens rather than defaulting to it. Flood is a separate policy in Florida, always.
Does House Insurance Cover Boiler Breakdown?

Generally no. [Does house insurance cover a boiler](/qa/does-house-insurance-cover-boiler/) depends on why it failed. If a boiler is damaged by fire, a storm, an [escape of water](/qa/water-leak-insurance-claim-uk/), or (with accidental damage cover) a knock during DIY, the buildings part of a home policy typically pays. If it stops working because it is old, worn out or poorly maintained, that is wear and tear, a standard exclusion on almost every policy. Breakdown protection comes from home emergency cover, a boiler cover plan, a manufacturer warranty or an equipment breakdown endorsement, and many of those require a documented annual service. In a leasehold flat, whether the boiler counts as part of the building or as your own fixture also depends on the lease, which is one more reason to check who insures what.
California Home Insurance in High Fire Risk Areas

Owners searching for [California home insurance in high fire risk areas](/qa/california-home-insurance-in-high-fire-risk-areas/) face a market in transition. After years of non-renewals, the state's Sustainable Insurance Strategy allows insurers to use forward-looking catastrophe models in exchange for writing more policies in wildfire-distressed areas, and the Safer from Wildfires regulation requires insurers and the [FAIR Plan](/compare/fair-plan-vs-admitted-homeowners-california/) to recognise verified mitigation such as ember-resistant vents, Class A roofing and defensible space. The FAIR Plan remains the insurer of last resort with basic fire-focused coverage, and many owners pair it with a difference-in-conditions (DIC) policy to fill the gaps. Reports indicate the FAIR Plan's approved average dwelling [rate increase](/qa/why-did-car-insurance-go-up-without-accidents/) of about 29.1% takes effect October 15, 2026, so this is the moment to document mitigation work and re-shop the policy - confirm current figures with the FAIR Plan or the California Department of Insurance.
What Does Farm Bureau Homeowners Insurance Cover?

There is no single national Farm Bureau policy. Farm Bureau insurers are separate state-based companies, so the answer to [what does Farm Bureau homeowners insurance cover](/qa/what-does-farm-bureau-homeowners-insurance-cover/) depends on your state's company. The common core matches any standard homeowners policy: dwelling, other structures such as sheds and detached garages, personal property, loss of use (additional living expenses), personal liability and medical payments to others. Many Farm Bureau companies also offer optional [endorsements](/learn/what-is-an-insurance-endorsement/) such as extended replacement cost, scheduled personal property for jewellery and similar items, and equipment or home systems cover, and some add account discounts for [bundling](/compare/home-auto-bundling-discount-savings/) with auto. Flood and earthquake remain separate, and farm buildings and livestock generally need a farm or ranch policy rather than a standard homeowners form.
The Pattern Behind All Seven Questions

Notice the recurring structure: a policy pays for sudden, accidental loss to the specific layer it insures, and excludes wear and tear, gradual damage and the layers someone else insures. Understanding [replacement cost versus actual cash value](/compare/actual-cash-value-vs-replacement-cost/), knowing what an [exclusion](/glossary/exclusion/) is, and choosing a [deductible](/glossary/deductible/) you could actually pay on a bad day will do more for you than chasing a marginally cheaper quote. If a claim ever goes sideways, the process in [first-party insurance claims](/learn/first-party-insurance-claims/) applies to home losses too, and [when to hire an insurance lawyer](/learn/when-to-hire-an-insurance-lawyer/) explains when a dispute needs professional help. And if a single loss could exceed your policy's liability limits, check whether an [umbrella policy](/learn/umbrella-insurance-guide/) makes sense using the [Coverage Ratio Calculator](/coverage-calculator/).
Which of These Questions Are Covered in Depth Elsewhere?

items: [Home and Auto Insurance Near Me: How to Find and Price a Bundle](/qa/home-and-auto-insurance-near-me/) - agent types, bundling discounts and the checks that stop a cheap bundle from being underinsured
[Do I Need Building Insurance for a Leasehold Flat?](/qa/do-i-need-building-insurance-for-a-leasehold-flat/) - who arranges the block policy, what it covers, and your rights to see it
[Do I Need Home Insurance If I Have Body Corporate?](/qa/do-i-need-home-insurance-if-i-have-body-corporate/) - what strata cover leaves out and who pays the excess
[Yesenia's Hialeah Home Insurance Quotes](/scenarios/yesenia-hialeah-home-insurance-quotes/) - a real-numbers walk-through of roof age, inspections and the Citizens comparison
[Does House Insurance Cover Boiler Breakdown?](/qa/does-house-insurance-cover-boiler/) - covered perils, wear and tear, and the breakdown options that actually pay
[California Home Insurance in High Fire Risk Areas](/qa/california-home-insurance-in-high-fire-risk-areas/) - FAIR Plan, DIC layering and wildfire mitigation credits
[What Does Farm Bureau Homeowners Insurance Cover?](/qa/what-does-farm-bureau-homeowners-insurance-cover/) - the state-by-state structure, core coverages and common endorsements

content.text: This article is educational and general in nature and does not constitute insurance, legal or financial advice. Property insurance rules, premiums and regulations vary by country, state, insurer and policy wording, and market conditions such as California FAIR Plan and Florida Citizens rates change frequently. Confirm details with your policy documents, your lease or scheme rules, your insurer and a licensed professional in your jurisdiction.

articles.title: Gap Insurance: Is It Worth It and How Much Does It Cost?
articles.description: Gap insurance pays what you still owe after a total loss. Learn when gap insurance is worth it, what it costs, and where to buy it cheaply.
articles.author: Insurance Bhaiya Research Desk
tags: how much is gap insurance for a car
keyTakeaways: Gap insurance pays the difference between what your car was worth (its actual cash value) and what you still owe on the loan or lease when the car is totaled or stolen — nothing more.

Gap insurance is worth it when you owe more than the car is worth: a small down payment, a loan of 60 months or longer, a fast-depreciating model, or negative equity rolled in from a trade-in. It is usually not worth it with a large down payment or a short loan.

Where you buy it matters far more than the product itself: an add-on to your auto policy typically runs about $20 to $60 a year, while a dealership contract commonly costs $400 to $700 up front and is often rolled into the loan, so you pay interest on it.
Most people only need gap coverage for one to three years, until the car is worth more than the balance, and prepaid gap is generally refundable pro rata if you pay off, refinance, or sell early.

Gap insurance often does not cover your collision or comprehensive deductible, late payments and fees, or add-ons like extended warranties, so read the contract rather than assuming it makes you whole.

faqs.question: Is gap insurance required by law?
faqs.answer: No state requires it. It's optional insurance, though a lender or leasing company may require it as a condition of financing, and many leases already include it.

faqs.question: Does gap insurance pay if my car is repaired instead of totaled?
faqs.answer: No. Gap only applies when the car is declared a total loss or stolen and not recovered. Repairable damage is handled by your collision or comprehensive coverage.

faqs.question: How long do I need gap insurance?
faqs.answer: Typically one to three years, or until your loan balance drops below the car's actual cash value. Check your payoff against a current valuation periodically, then cancel if you no longer need it.

content.text: [Gap insurance](/glossary/gap-insurance/) is one of the most misunderstood add-ons in car buying. Dealers pitch it as essential, some drivers assume it's a scam, and both are wrong in specific situations. This guide covers the two questions people actually search — **is gap insurance worth it** and **how much is gap insurance for a car** — plus the practical follow-ups: where to buy it, whether you can add it later, how it differs from new car replacement coverage, and how to cancel it for a refund.
What Gap Insurance Actually Does

When a car is totaled or stolen, your collision or [comprehensive coverage](/compare/comprehensive-vs-collision/) pays its actual cash value (ACV) — what the car was worth the moment before the loss — minus your deductible. If you owe more than that on your loan or lease, you're personally responsible for the difference. Gap (guaranteed asset protection) coverage pays that shortfall. It protects the loan, not the car.

rows: Loan payoff at the time of the total loss
Paid by your auto insurer (ACV minus deductible)
Remaining loan balance without gap insurance
Typically paid by gap (payoff minus ACV)
Typically left for you (the deductible, if your gap contract excludes it)

content.text: Notice that gap pays nothing if the ACV already covers the loan. It only matters in the early years, when depreciation outpaces your loan paydown. You also need comprehensive and collision coverage for gap to have anything to sit on top of — see [does car insurance cover repairs](/qa/does-car-insurance-cover-repairs/) for how those two coverages work.
Is Gap Insurance Worth It?

It depends entirely on whether you're likely to owe more than the car is worth. A quick test: if your loan balance is higher than what the car would sell for today, you're 'upside down' and gap has real value. Our full breakdown is in [is gap insurance worth it](/qa/is-gap-insurance-worth-it/).

items: **Usually worth it:** down payment under about 20%, loan term of 60 months or longer, a model that depreciates quickly, negative equity rolled in from a trade-in, or a lease that doesn't already include it.
**Usually not worth it:** a large down payment, a short loan, a car that's already worth more than you owe, or a vehicle you bought outright.

content.text: How Much Is Gap Insurance for a Car?

rows: Add-on to your auto insurance policy
Often a flat fee or added to the loan
One-time charge, frequently rolled into the loan (you pay interest on it)

content.text: The same core protection can cost ten times more at a dealership. The full comparison, including what drives the price up or down, is in [how much is gap insurance for a car](/qa/how-much-is-gap-insurance-for-a-car/). To see what your insurer would actually charge, use our [Car Insurance Coverage Calculator](/car-insurance-calculator/) and read [the best rate on car insurance](/qa/best-rate-on-car-insurance/) for how to compare quotes properly.
Can You Buy Gap Insurance After You've Already Bought the Car?

Often yes, but the window depends on who sells it. Insurer add-ons commonly require a fairly new vehicle and may limit how long after purchase you can add coverage, while lender and dealership products may only be offered at signing. See [can you buy gap insurance after buying a car](/qa/can-you-buy-gap-insurance-after-buying-a-car/).
Gap Insurance vs. New Car Replacement Coverage

These two are frequently confused. Gap pays off your loan; new car replacement pays toward a brand-new equivalent car, usually only in the first year or two of ownership. See the side-by-side in [gap insurance vs. new car replacement coverage](/compare/gap-insurance-vs-new-car-replacement/).
How to Cancel Gap Insurance and Get a Refund

If you prepaid gap and then pay off the loan early, refinance, or trade the car in, you can generally get a pro-rata refund of the unused portion, but you usually have to ask. Walkthrough: [how to cancel gap insurance and get a refund](/qa/how-to-cancel-gap-insurance-and-get-a-refund/).
What Gap Insurance Usually Does Not Cover

items: Your collision or comprehensive deductible (some contracts include a small deductible credit; many don't)
Late payments, missed-payment fees, and related loan charges
Credit insurance and similar charges rolled into the loan
Extended warranties and service contracts financed with the car
A rental car while yours is being replaced — see [how long insurance pays for a rental car after an accident](/qa/how-long-will-insurance-pay-for-rental-car-after-accident/)

articles.title: How Much Is Motorcycle Insurance? Average Cost by Age, Bike Type & State (2026)
articles.description: How much is motorcycle insurance? See 2026 average costs for minimum and full coverage by age, bike type and state, plus the 7 factors that set your price.
articles.author: Insurance Bhaiya Research Desk
keyTakeaways: The national average cost of motorcycle insurance is about $141 a year for minimum coverage and $364 a year for full coverage, according to [MoneyGeek's 2026 data](https://www.moneygeek.com/insurance/motorcycle/average-cost-of-motorcycle-insurance/).
Age matters enormously. A 16-year-old pays roughly $1,446 a year for full coverage, compared with about $571 at age 40, in the same dataset.

Bike type is the single biggest lever. Sport bikes can cost several times more than a standard or cruiser. [IIHS](https://www.iihs.org/topics/motorcycles) finds supersport riders die at about 4 times the rate of cruiser and standard riders.

State matters too. Median premiums range from about $9 a month in Kansas and Montana to about $35 in New Jersey. See our [Colorado](/qa/how-much-is-motorcycle-insurance-in-colorado/) and [Ohio](/qa/how-much-is-motorcycle-insurance-in-ohio/) breakdowns.

Motorcycle insurance usually costs far less than car insurance, about 59% to 76% less on average, but it protects you far less in a crash. See [motorcycle insurance vs car insurance](/compare/motorcycle-insurance-vs-car-insurance/).

faqs.question: How much is motorcycle insurance a month?
faqs.answer: On average, about $12 a month for minimum coverage and about $30 a month for full coverage, based on MoneyGeek's 2026 national data. Young riders and sport-bike owners often pay $100 to $300 a month or more.

faqs.question: Is motorcycle insurance cheaper than car insurance?
faqs.answer: Usually, yes. Motorcycle insurance averages roughly 59% to 76% less than car insurance, depending on coverage level. It covers you less in a crash, though. See [motorcycle insurance vs car insurance](/compare/motorcycle-insurance-vs-car-insurance/).

faqs.question: Why is my motorcycle insurance so expensive?
faqs.answer: The usual culprits are a sport or supersport bike, being under 25, a recent ticket or crash, urban parking in a high-theft area, or a low deductible. Change any one of those and your quote can drop sharply.

faqs.question: Does motorcycle insurance cost less in winter?
faqs.answer: It can, if your insurer offers [lay-up coverage](/glossary/lay-up-coverage/). This keeps comprehensive active while the bike is stored and pauses the riding coverages, so you pay less without a lapse.

content.text: If you're shopping for your first bike, or you've just seen a renewal quote that made you wince, you want one number: **how much is motorcycle insurance**, really? The honest answer is that it depends more than car insurance does. Two riders on the same street can pay $90 and $2,000 for the same year of cover. In this guide we give you the averages, show you exactly why your quote lands where it does, and explain how to bring it down without leaving yourself exposed. It's part of our [Motorcycle, Dirt Bike & Powersport Insurance hub](/learn/motorcycle-dirt-bike-powersport-insurance/).
Average Cost of Motorcycle Insurance in 2026

rows: Pays others you injure or whose property you damage. Nothing for your bike or your own injuries
Liability plus [comprehensive and collision](/compare/comprehensive-vs-collision/) for your own bike

content.text: Source: [MoneyGeek national motorcycle rate analysis, 2026](https://www.moneygeek.com/insurance/motorcycle/average-cost-of-motorcycle-insurance/). [ValuePenguin](https://www.valuepenguin.com/average-cost-of-motorcycle-insurance) arrives at a similar national average of about $399 a year ($33 a month). Both studies price a sample rider, typically a middle-aged rider with a clean record on a standard bike. If that's not you, your price will differ, sometimes by a lot. Not sure whether you need [full coverage](/learn/car-insurance-guide/) or just liability? Read [full coverage vs liability-only motorcycle insurance](/compare/full-coverage-vs-liability-only-motorcycle-insurance/) first.
Motorcycle Insurance Cost by Age

Insurers price young riders the way they price young drivers, only more steeply. Crash data explains why: riders under 25 crash more, and motorcycle crashes are rarely minor. [NHTSA](https://www.nhtsa.gov/road-safety/motorcycles) reports that in 2024, per mile traveled, motorcyclists were almost 27 times more likely than car occupants to die in a crash. MoneyGeek's figures put full coverage at about **$1,446 a year for a 16-year-old** and about **$571 a year for a 40-year-old**. Rates usually fall steadily through the 20s and flatten out by your mid-30s, as long as your record stays clean.

content.title: Under 25? Here's What Actually Moves the Needle
content.text: Take a certified rider course (find one at the [Motorcycle Safety Foundation](https://msf-usa.org/)). Start on a 300cc to 650cc standard instead of a supersport. Get your full endorsement rather than riding on a permit, which matters in [can you get motorcycle insurance without a license](/qa/can-you-get-motorcycle-insurance-without-a-license/). Consider a higher deductible. Want to see all four in action? Follow [Rohan's first sport bike scenario](/scenarios/rohan-first-sport-bike-texas/).
Motorcycle Insurance Cost by Bike Type

headers: Why Insurers Price It That Way
rows: Low speeds, low value, cheap parts
Relaxed riding position, older rider base, lower crash rates
High purchase price and expensive parts drive collision and comprehensive costs
High speed, young rider base, roughly 4x the fatality rate (IIHS), high theft appeal
Street liability plus off-road use. See [dirt bike insurance coverage](/learn/dirt-bike-insurance-coverage/)

content.text: To show how wide the gap can be, MoneyGeek's example priced a sport bike's full coverage at about **$329 a month**, against about **$30 a month** for a standard motorcycle with the same rider. Nothing else you control comes close to that effect.
Motorcycle Insurance Cost by State

Your state sets the legal minimum and your ZIP code sets your theft and traffic risk. Both show up in the premium. Median monthly premiums run from about $9 in Kansas and Montana to about $35 in New Jersey (MoneyGeek). ValuePenguin lists Kentucky, Florida, Arizona, Mississippi and Texas among the most expensive states. Theft is a big part of the story. The [NICB](https://www.nicb.org/news/news-releases/lock-your-bikes-motorcycle-thefts-rise-third-consecutive-year) ranks California, Florida and Texas as the top three states for motorcycle theft, and theft risk is priced straight into comprehensive coverage. Dig into specific states here:

items: [How much is motorcycle insurance in Colorado?](/qa/how-much-is-motorcycle-insurance-in-colorado/) Minimum 25/50/15. About $117 a year minimum and $567 full coverage.
[How much is motorcycle insurance in Ohio?](/qa/how-much-is-motorcycle-insurance-in-ohio/) Minimum 25/50/25. Roughly $115 to $315 a year minimum.
[Do you need insurance on a motorcycle in Florida?](/qa/do-you-need-insurance-on-a-motorcycle-in-florida/) Not required to register, but expensive to go without.

content.text: The 7 Factors That Set Your Motorcycle Insurance Price

items: **Bike type and engine size.** The biggest factor by far.
**Age and riding experience.** Years with a full endorsement count, not just your age.

**Riding and driving record.** A DUI can raise full-coverage rates by around 68% (MoneyGeek). At-fault crashes linger for years. See [how long does an accident stay on your insurance](/qa/how-long-does-an-accident-stay-on-your-insurance/).

**Where you live and park.** Urban street parking in a high-theft metro costs the most. How theft claims pay out is covered in [does motorcycle insurance cover theft](/qa/does-motorcycle-insurance-cover-theft/).
**Coverage choices.** Liability-only is cheapest. Adding [custom parts and equipment coverage](/glossary/custom-parts-and-equipment-coverage/), passenger cover and roadside assistance adds cost.
**Deductibles.** Higher deductibles lower the premium. Find your break-even with the [deductible vs premium calculator](/deductible-calculator/).
**Seasonality.** Riders in cold states can save with [lay-up coverage](/glossary/lay-up-coverage/) instead of paying for 12 months of full cover on a bike that sits for five.

content.text: How to Get Cheap Motorcycle Insurance Without Being Underinsured

There's a right way and a wrong way to cut your premium. The wrong way is dropping to state minimums when you have savings or home equity to protect, or skipping uninsured motorist coverage. Those are the coverages that pay for the worst day of your life. The right way looks like this:

items: **Shop at least three quotes with identical limits.** Prices for the same rider can vary by hundreds of dollars between insurers.
**Bundle** with your car or home policy. Multi-policy discounts are common.
**Drop collision on an older bike** once its value falls below roughly 10 times the annual collision premium.
**Protect your passenger properly** instead of over-buying extras. Read [does motorcycle insurance cover passengers](/qa/does-motorcycle-insurance-cover-passengers/).

**Financing a new bike?** Price in [gap insurance](/glossary/gap-insurance/) now. Find out why in [the financed-bike total-loss scenario](/scenarios/financed-motorcycle-totaled-owes-more-than-value/).
**Check your limits against your net worth** with the [coverage gap checker](/coverage-gap-checker/).
